issues.legal_issue: A law abolishing personal inams and extinguishing rights in them is constitutionally valid despite the absence of compensation in the law and does not impermissibly vary the terms of a grant recognizing the inam.
material_facts: The holder had acquired a personal inam from the original inamdar, who had received a grant recognizing it.
The challenged law abolished personal inams and extinguished rights in them.

The holder argued that the law was not protected by the constitutional provision concerning estates because the property was not an estate and no compensation was provided, and that the grant could not be varied by legislation.
issues.conclusion: The constitutional challenge failed; the law was valid and protected by Article 31-A, and the grant did not prevent the State from legislating to alter the rights it recognized.
issues.legal_principle: The Court followed Gangadharrao Narayanrao Majumdar v. State of Bombay in upholding the law under Article 31-A. It rejected the argument that a grant recognizing an inam was immutable, following Thakur Jagannath Baksh Singh v. United Provinces and Maharaj Umeg Singh v. State of Bombay; Article 294(b) did not prevent the legislation.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_inam_aboliti: A person challenges the constitutionality of a law that abolishes personal inams.
predicates.personal_inam_rights_extinguished_by_law: The challenged law extinguishes rights held under a personal inam.
predicates.recognized_grant_challenged_as_immutable: The holder relies on a grant recognizing the inam to argue that legislation cannot alter its terms.
predicates.compensation_or_estate_objection_raised: The holder argues that the law lacks constitutional protection because the property is not an estate or the law provides no compensation.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge to an inam-abolition law concerns extinguished personal-inam rights and relies on either a recognized grant or an objection about estate status or compensation, the law is constitutionally valid.

issues.legal_issue: An exception protecting inam land used for building or other non-agricultural purposes from vesting in the State does not exempt that land from the provisions abolishing inams and requiring payment of land revenue.
material_facts: The holder's inam land was being used for building and other non-agricultural purposes.
The law provided that certain parts of inam lands vested in the State, with an exception for land used by the inamdar for building or other non-agricultural purposes.
The holder argued that the exception removed the land from the law's provisions abolishing the inam and requiring payment of land revenue.
issues.conclusion: The exception only prevented the specified land from vesting in the State; the land remained subject to the provisions abolishing the inam and requiring payment of land revenue.
issues.legal_principle: The Court read the vesting provision and its exception as addressing only whether the specified land vested in the State. The exception did not displace the separate provisions abolishing personal inams and making inam land liable to land revenue.

predicates.inam_revenue_assessment_dispute: A dispute concerns the revenue treatment of land formerly held as an inam.
predicates.inam_land_used_for_building_or_nonagricu: The inam land is used for a building or another non-agricultural purpose.
predicates.land_saved_from_state_vesting: An exception prevents the land from vesting in the State.

issues.definition: When inam land used for building or another non-agricultural purpose is saved from vesting, it remains subject to inam abolition and land revenue.

issues.legal_issue: Land that becomes liable to full land revenue after abolition of the inam must be assessed according to its use at the time of assessment, regardless of when its non-agricultural use began.
material_facts: The holder's land had previously been held as a personal inam and was not then subject to full assessment.
After the inam was abolished, the land became liable to full assessment under the applicable revenue law.
At the time assessment was to be made, the land was being used for a building rather than agriculture.
The holder disputed assessment on a non-agricultural basis and relied on the history of the land's use.
issues.conclusion: The land was assessable as non-agricultural land according to its use when assessment was made; when that use began was immaterial.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 5 of the Bombay Personal Inams Abolition Act and 45 and 48 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, inam land became liable to full land revenue, and assessment depended on the land's use at the time of assessment. The assessment category followed the current use, not the date that use began.

predicates.inam_revenue_assessment_dispute: A dispute concerns the revenue assessment of land formerly held as an inam.
predicates.land_becomes_liable_to_full_revenue: The land becomes liable to full land revenue after the special inam treatment ends.
predicates.land_currently_used_for_nonagricultural_: The land is being used for a non-agricultural purpose when assessment is made.

issues.definition: When land formerly held as an inam becomes liable to full revenue and is then used for a non-agricultural purpose, it must be assessed according to that current use.

issues.legal_issue: A provision barring a Collector from assessing land where an assessment has been fixed under a special settlement chapter refers to an assessment actually fixed under that chapter, not one deemed to have been fixed there by a deeming provision.
material_facts: The land was not wholly exempt from land revenue.
No assessment had in fact been fixed on the land under the special settlement chapter.
A deeming provision treated earlier revenue settlements as having been made under that chapter.
The Collector assessed the land under the provision empowering assessment of land not wholly exempt from revenue.
issues.conclusion: The deeming provision did not bar use of the Collector's assessment power; because no assessment had actually been fixed under the special settlement chapter and the land was not wholly exempt, the Collector could assess it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code excluded its application where an assessment had been fixed under Chapter VIII-A. The Court held that this referred to an actual assessment under that chapter, not an assessment deemed to have been made there under section 117-R. Since there was no actual assessment under the chapter and the land was not wholly exempt from revenue, section 52 applied.

rule.if: inam_revenue_assessment_dispute and land_not_wholly_exempt_from_revenue and no_actual_special_settlement_assessment and earlier_settlement_only_deemed_made_under_special_chapter

predicates.inam_revenue_assessment_dispute: A dispute concerns the Collector's assessment of land formerly held as an inam.
predicates.land_not_wholly_exempt_from_revenue: The land is not wholly exempt from the payment of land revenue.
predicates.no_actual_special_settlement_assessment: No assessment was actually fixed on the land under the special settlement process.
predicates.earlier_settlement_only_deemed_made_unde: An earlier settlement is treated as having been made under the special settlement process only by operation of a deeming rule.

issues.definition: When land is not wholly exempt, has no actual assessment under the special settlement process, and has only an earlier settlement deemed to be under that process, the Collector may assess it under the general assessment power.
